newsitem.title: CANADA: Canada separatist party choses new leader.
newsitem.headline: Canada separatist party choses new leader.

text.p: The Bloc Quebecois, a Quebec separatist party that forms the official opposition in Canada's parliament, chose former communist Gilles Duceppe as its new leader on Saturday.
The 49-year-old won the leadership with 53 percent of the ballots mailed in by party members. About 50,000 of the Bloc's 113,000 members voted.
Duceppe's victory over five other candidates, including two women, was announced at the party's three-day convention in Montreal.
Duceppe replaced Michel Gauthier, who stepped aside to give the Bloc a better chance of once again winning the majority of Quebec seats in the next federal election.

In his acceptance speech to the convention, Duceppe called for a "dialogue of equals" between Quebec and the rest of Canada. "The Bloc is essential for Canadians to know what Quebeckers want," Duceppe said.

Duceppe said the Bloc was ready to battle the federal Liberals headed by Canadian Prime Minister Jean Chretien for electoral supremacy in Quebec. "Friends, the campaign has begun. The Bloc will take stock of the Chretien government," he said.
Within moments of winning the leadership, Duceppe faced the immediate issue of party unity.

Bloc MP Nic LeBlanc told reporters he could not identify with Duceppe's communist past and would resign and serve as an independent, leaving the party with 50 seats -- the same number as the Western Canada-based Reform Party.
The move could jeopardize the Bloc's standing as official opposition party, although it will keep that status if it remains tied with the Reform Party.
Yves Duhaime, who came second with 34 percent of the vote, publicly rebuffed his new leader, saying he did not think he was the man to lead the party. "He's not my type," he said.
Duhaime refused to confirm that, as planned, he would be the Bloc candidate in the home electoral district of Prime Minister Chretien in the election, which is expected to be called for June 9.

With the Bloc Quebecois in Canada's parliament and the separatist Parti Quebecois in power in Quebec, the province's drive for independence has been at the forefront of Canadian politics for the past six years.

The Bloc Quebecois was formed in 1990 when Lucien Bouchard, Quebec premier, left the federal Progressive Conservative party in frustration with the lack of movement on reforms that would give the French-speaking province special constitutional status in Canada.

The Bloc worked closely with the Parti Quebecois during the October 1995 referedum on Quebec sovereignty, which separatists lost by one percentage point. Bouchard has said he plans to hold another referendum on sovereignty after the next Quebec provincial election, which could be held in 1998.

After Bouchard left the Bloc to become Quebec premier in January 1996, there was speculation about whether the party would be able retain its official opposition status after the next federal election.
Recent polls show that despite a possible resurgence by the Conservatives under its Quebec-based leader Jean Charest, the Bloc could still win a majority of Quebec seats.
